content: The underlying mechanisms of what is referred to as cough variant asthma have not been extensively studied, and there is ongoing debate among experts regarding whether this condition should truly be classified as asthma. Advocates for the concept of cough variant asthma often recommend a trial of asthma-specific treatments to assess their effectiveness. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of inhaled beta2-agonists in managing non-specific chronic cough in children aged over 2 years. To gather relevant data, comprehensive searches were conducted in databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additionally, reference lists were reviewed, trial authors were contacted, and unpublished or non-peer-reviewed literature, including theses and internal reports, was sought. The search was last updated in February 2006. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled clinical trials in which inhaled beta2-agonists were administered to children over 2 years of age with chronic cough. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and methodological quality of the studies. Data from trials comparing salbutamol to placebo were extracted by both reviewers and analyzed using the Cochrane Collaboration's Review Manager software, version 4.2. The results indicated that, in children with isolated chronic cough, there was no statistically significant difference in outcomes between the group treated with salbutamol and the placebo group. The authors concluded that salbutamol does not differ from placebo in its ability to reduce the frequency of cough, whether measured objectively or subjectively.
